blocks.text: Not every prompt template is a fixed slab of text waiting for a couple of blanks to be filled in.
Some prompts change shape depending on what is happening on the server right now, what files are currently open, which branch is checked out, what tickets are in the queue.

These are dynamic prompts, and they are one of the places MCP quietly earns its keep, letting a server offer a shortcut that stays accurate to the present moment instead of describing a world that may no longer exist.
This lesson contrasts dynamic prompts with the static templates from the previous lesson, and looks at exactly where that runtime dependence is allowed to live.
1. Static Templates vs Dynamic Prompts

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A static template is compared against a dynamic prompt built from live state

blocks.text: A static prompt template is the kind covered in the last lesson: its name, description, and argument list are fixed the moment the server is written, and they do not change from one prompts/list call to the next. A dynamic prompt is different in one specific way, some part of what the server reports back, the arguments it offers, the description it shows, or the content it fills in, depends on state that can change while the server is running.

Both kinds are still prompts in the exact same protocol sense, same prompts/list, same prompts/get, same message shaped result. The difference is entirely about where the values inside that shape come from, a fixed string written once by the server author, or a value computed fresh each time based on what is currently true.

It helps to think of a static prompt as a printed form and a dynamic prompt as a form that a clerk fills in the currently valid options for right before handing it to you. The paper itself, the protocol shape, is identical either way, what differs is whether someone checked today's facts before handing it over.
2. What "Runtime State" Means Here
Runtime state is anything that can be different between two calls made minutes apart without the server itself being redeployed or rewritten.
The current contents of a project folder, the currently checked out git branch, the number of unresolved support tickets, the identity of the user currently connected, all of these are runtime state.
A dynamic prompt reads from this state at the moment it is asked for, rather than baking in an answer that was true only when the server was first written.

It is useful to separate runtime state from configuration. A server's configured behavior, which database it connects to, which model it defers to, is normally set once at startup and rarely changes without a redeploy. Runtime state is the opposite, it is exactly the kind of thing that is expected to shift many times over a single day the server stays running.
3. Example: A Prompt That Lists Current Project Files

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A server reads current project files and builds a prompt around them

blocks.text: Consider a coding assistant server exposing a prompt named summarize_file. A static version of this prompt would simply take a file path as a free-typed string argument, with no help guessing what paths actually exist. A dynamic version instead looks at the project directory right now, and turns its list of arguments, or an enum-like set of suggested values, into something that reflects the files that genuinely exist at this moment.

Five minutes later, after a new file has been added and one deleted, the exact same prompts/list call could return a different suggested set of paths in that same description. Nothing about the protocol changed, only the state the server consulted while building its response.
3.1 Why Not Just Let the User Type Any Path

A free-typed file path argument still works, of course, MCP does not forbid it. The value dynamic discovery adds is reducing guesswork, a user who does not remember the exact spelling of a nested path benefits enormously from seeing the current, real options spelled out, rather than having to go check a file browser separately before coming back to use the prompt.
4. Where the Dynamism Lives: On the Server, Not the Client

It is worth being precise about this: the client never computes anything dynamic itself. It always just asks prompts/list and receives whatever the server currently reports. All of the logic that inspects the file system, checks a database, or reads a queue lives entirely inside the server's handling of that request. This keeps the client's job exactly as simple for a dynamic prompt as it is for a static one, ask, receive, display.

This separation of concerns is also why dynamic prompts do not require any new client capability or protocol feature to work. A client that already correctly implements static prompt handling will, without any additional code, correctly handle a dynamic prompt too, because the wire format never distinguishes between the two.
5. Dynamic Argument Lists

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: The argument list itself can be computed dynamically per request

blocks.text: The most common form of dynamism is a description that mentions currently valid values, since MCP's prompt arguments do not have a formal enum type. A server can compute this list at the moment prompts/list is called, and simply write it into the argument's description text, giving the user something concrete to choose from rather than a blank free text field.

code.content: { "name": "ticket_id", "description": "Currently open tickets: TICKET-401, TICKET-402, TICKET-415", "required": true }

blocks.text: Because MCP prompt arguments are plain strings rather than a strict enum type, a server cannot force a client to only submit one of the listed values, it can only suggest them clearly in the description and validate what actually arrives once prompts/get is called. This is one more reason validation on the server side, covered fully in the next lesson, matters just as much for dynamic prompts as for static ones.
6. Dynamic Descriptions

A prompt's top level description can also shift with state, not just its arguments' descriptions. A deployment assistant prompt named deploy_current_branch might describe itself differently depending on which branch is actually checked out right now, "Deploys the feature/login-fix branch to staging" this minute, "Deploys the main branch to production" the next, without the prompt's name ever changing.

A subtler version of this is a description that adjusts its tone or emphasis based on urgency, a monitoring server's check_service_health prompt might describe itself calmly during normal operation and far more pointedly the moment an actual outage is detected, without its name or its arguments changing at all.
7. Dynamic Content Inside the Filled Messages

Dynamism can also show up after prompts/get is called, inside the actual filled messages a server returns, not just inside the earlier prompts/list listing. A prompt might pull in the current date, the current user's name, or a live count of something, and weave it directly into the message text it hands back, on top of whatever arguments the client explicitly supplied.

This kind of content injection blurs pleasantly into the territory covered later in this module under context injection, where a prompt pulls in an entire resource's contents rather than just a date or a count. The core idea is the same, computing something at fill time rather than baking it in ahead of time, just applied at a larger scale.
8. The prompts/list Call Still Looks the Same

From a protocol standpoint, a dynamic prompt's prompts/list response is structurally identical to a static one, same fields, same shape. There is no special flag marking a prompt as dynamic. A client cannot tell, just by looking at one response, whether the values it received are guaranteed to be identical next time or not, which is exactly why treating every value as potentially fresh is the safer default.

This uniformity is a deliberate design choice in MCP. Rather than introducing a separate mechanism for dynamic prompts, the protocol simply lets any field be recomputed at call time, keeping the number of concepts a client author has to learn as small as possible.
9. When prompts/list Itself Changes: The list_changed Notification

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A server sends a list changed notification when its prompt list changes

blocks.text: Sometimes the change is bigger than a description's wording, an entire prompt might appear or disappear, for example a deploy_hotfix prompt that only exists while an incident is active. When a server's available prompts shift meaningfully, it can send a prompts/list_changed notification, telling any connected client that it is worth calling prompts/list again rather than trusting a stale cached copy.

A server should be judicious about firing this notification too, sending it on every tiny state change can flood a client with refresh requests it does not actually need to act on. A reasonable habit is to send it only when a prompt has genuinely appeared, disappeared, or had its argument list meaningfully altered, not for every minor wording tweak to a description.

A client receiving this notification does not need to do anything more complicated than call prompts/list again and refresh whatever it is displaying, the same simple request response pattern used everywhere else in the protocol.
10. A Server Watching Its Own State

Implementing a dynamic prompt usually means the server has some existing piece of code, a file watcher, a webhook handler, a polling loop, that already tracks the relevant state for its own purposes. Exposing that state through a prompt is often just a matter of reading from the same source the server already consults elsewhere, rather than building anything new from scratch.

This also means dynamic prompts add real implementation cost that a static prompt does not have, the server needs a reliable way to answer "what is true right now" quickly enough that a prompts/list call does not noticeably lag. Poorly implemented state lookups can make an otherwise fast server feel sluggish the moment a dynamic prompt is added.
11. Example: A Prompt Tied to the Current Git Branch

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A prompt reads the current git branch before it is filled

blocks.text: A development tools server might expose a prompt named write_commit_message whose description always names the branch currently checked out, "Writes a commit message for changes on feature/checkout-flow". Behind the scenes, the server runs a quick git command every time prompts/list is called, so the description is never more than a moment out of date.
11.1 Combining Several Live Signals

Nothing stops a server from blending more than one live signal into a single dynamic description, naming both the current branch and how many files it touches compared to main, for instance. The guiding principle stays the same as with any prompt design, only include a detail if it genuinely helps a user decide whether and how to use the prompt right now.
12. Static Prompts: The Simple Baseline Still Matters

None of this means static prompts are a lesser option, plenty of genuinely useful prompts have no runtime dependence at all, a fixed checklist for writing a postmortem, a fixed structure for a weekly status update. When a prompt's value comes entirely from good, stable wording rather than from reflecting some changing fact, keeping it static is simpler to build, simpler to reason about, and simpler to cache.

A good exercise when reviewing a set of prompts a server offers is to ask, for each one, whether making it dynamic would meaningfully improve it, or whether it is only being made dynamic because the capability exists. Not every prompt benefits from reflecting live state, and forcing dynamism onto a prompt that does not need it is wasted engineering effort.
13. Choosing Static vs Dynamic When Designing a Prompt

blocks.content: {"headers":["Question","If yes, lean toward"],"rows":[["Does the prompt's usefulness depend on data that changes minute to minute?","Dynamic"],["Is the wording good today and still good next year unchanged?","Static"],["Would a user benefit from seeing currently valid choices before typing an argument?","Dynamic"],["Is the entire value of the prompt in its fixed structure, not in reflecting current facts?","Static"]]}

blocks.text: Many real prompts end up as a mix, a mostly static structure with one or two dynamic touches, a fixed checklist template whose description simply names how many items are currently on it. Treating this as a spectrum rather than a strict either or choice usually leads to better design decisions than forcing every prompt into one category.
14. Risks of Too Much Dynamism

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: Too much dynamism can make prompt behavior unpredictable

blocks.text: Pulling too much live state into a prompt can backfire. A description crammed with twenty currently open ticket numbers is harder to read than one that simply says "enter a ticket ID", and a prompt whose behavior shifts noticeably from one moment to the next can feel unpredictable to a user who expects the same shortcut to behave the same way every time they reach for it.

blocks.title: Balance is the goal
blocks.content: Use dynamism to make a prompt more accurate and more helpful, not to cram every available fact into a description just because the data happens to be available.

blocks.text: 14.1 Predictability Is a Feature

Users build muscle memory around prompts they use often. A prompt whose description reads noticeably differently every single time undermines that muscle memory, even when each individual description is accurate. Aim for dynamism that adds a small, clearly useful detail on top of an otherwise stable, recognizable shape.
15. Caching Considerations for Dynamic Prompts

A client that caches prompts/list results for performance needs to be more careful with a server known to expose dynamic prompts, since a cached copy can go stale the moment underlying state changes. Respecting prompts/list_changed notifications, and generally treating a dynamic prompt's cached data as short lived, keeps a client from showing a user options that no longer make sense.

A practical compromise many servers use is a short lived cache, a few seconds to a minute, long enough to avoid recomputing expensive state on every keystroke of a fast-typing user browsing a prompt picker, short enough that the data shown is still functionally fresh.
16. Dynamic Prompts and the Client's Mental Model

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A dynamic prompt can surprise a client that expects stable behavior

blocks.text: None of this dynamism changes how a client is expected to behave. It still calls prompts/list, still shows a user a name and description, still collects arguments, still calls prompts/get. The only difference dynamic prompts introduce is that a client should not assume the exact same result will come back if it asks again later, an assumption that was already mostly true for well designed static prompts but is now explicitly not guaranteed.

In practice, most client implementations handle this simply by never assuming prompts/list results are permanent, refetching on a reasonable interval or in response to a list_changed notification, and displaying whatever comes back without trying to diff it against a remembered previous version.
Worked Example
A project management server exposes a prompt named triage_ticket. Its description is computed fresh on every prompts/list call by querying the ticket database for tickets tagged urgent right now.

The prompt's name and its overall purpose never change, only the live detail baked into its description, which is exactly the kind of narrow, well scoped dynamism that makes a prompt genuinely more useful without making it unpredictable.

This pattern generalizes well beyond ticket triage, any prompt that references a small, currently relevant set of items, open pull requests, active incidents, unread messages, can use the exact same recompute-on-list approach without needing any special protocol support.
Common Mistakes

items: Computing expensive state on every single prompts/list call when a short cache would be perfectly safe.
Forgetting to send a prompts/list_changed notification when a prompt appears or disappears based on state.
Cramming so much live data into a description that it becomes harder to read than a plain static one would have been.
Assuming a client will always re-fetch prompts/list before every use, rather than relying on notifications to prompt a refresh.
Making a prompt's core behavior, not just its description, change unpredictably between calls in ways a user cannot anticipate.
Building dynamism into a prompt that would have worked perfectly well as a simple static template.

blocks.text: When in doubt, start a new prompt as static, and only introduce dynamism once a concrete, specific benefit to the user becomes clear. It is far easier to add dynamism later than to walk back a prompt that has become unpredictable.
Practice

Design a dynamic prompt for a server that manages a shared calendar. The prompt should help a user schedule a meeting, and its description should reflect the next three genuinely free time slots, computed at the moment prompts/list is called.

As a stretch goal, decide what a reasonable prompts/list_changed policy would be for this calendar server, should it notify on every single booking, or only when the set of free slots shown in the description changes meaningfully.
Key Takeaway

A dynamic prompt looks exactly like a static one at the protocol level, same prompts/list, same prompts/get, but some part of what it reports, an argument's valid values, a description, or the filled content itself, is computed fresh from runtime state rather than fixed once and for all. That state always lives and gets read on the server, the client's job stays unchanged.

The next lesson goes deeper on prompt arguments themselves, required versus optional, how types are described, and what a well behaved server does when it receives a request missing a required argument or holding an invalid one.

Carry that same instinct, prefer the simplest thing that genuinely serves the user, into how you think about arguments next, since deciding what to make required, optional, or validated follows the exact same logic.
